newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Sacked premier Tshisekedi is Mobutu's arch-foe.
newsitem.headline: Sacked premier Tshisekedi is Mobutu's arch-foe.

text.p: Opposition firebrand Etienne Tshisekedi, sacked for the second time in four years as Zaire prime minister, is a one-time ally of President Mobutu Sese Seko who became one of his most implacable foes.

Tshisekedi was reappointed to his job last week. But, in typical fashion, he immediately clashed headlong with Mobutu supporters and his own allies by excluding all but his close loyalists from a new cabinet.
So, instead of stabilising a shaky government to deal with rebels who have seized more than a half of the vast country, his appointment plunged Zaire into deeper turmoil.
His teeming army of fanatical township followers clashed with security forces in the capital on Tuesday and Wednesday after it became clear Tshisekedi was about to be dropped.
Mobutu invoked emergency powers he decreed on Tuesday to appoint army general Likulia Bolongo to replace Tshisekedi.
For his supporters from the overcrowded slums of the capital Kinshasa, Tshisekedi is the staunchest and most incorruptible opponent of Mobutu.
They see the burly leader of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) as the one man who has stood up to Mobutu in public, in government, and in face-to-face meetings.
"We won't take this lying down. They will find us in their path," a Tshisekedi supporter said on hearing of the sacking.
Tshisekedi has gone to some lengths to cultivate his image as a man of the people, avoiding the typical excesses of Zaire's ruling elite. He drives a modest Peugeot.
But some diplomats question his democratic credentials while rivals blame him for the fragmentation the political opposition.

Tshisekedi, 64, is a native of diamond-rich Kasai Province, whose capital Mbuji-Mayi fell to Laurent Kabila's rebels last week. Kabila tried to woo Tshisekedi followers when he addressed a rally in Mbuji-Mayi on Tuesday, calling on the opposition leader to make a clean break with Mobutu -- their common enemy.
Tshisekedi spent his formative political years as both a diplomat and a minister of Mobutu, who has ruled since 1965.
He spearheaded domestic calls for multi-party politics which, coupled with pressure from abroad, forced a reluctant Mobutu to start to open the door to democracy in 1990.
At the height of the campaign for democracy he denounced Mobutu as a "human monster" and called for the president to flee the country or stand trial for corruption and other crimes.

In 1991 Mobutu, under foreign pressure to introduce democratic reform, appointed him first state commissar (prime minister). Mobutu dismissed him 12 days later when he refused to swear an oath of allegiance to him.
A sovereign national conference elected Tshisekedi prime minister in 1992. Mobutu sacked him again in 1993 but this time Tshisekedi refused to go -- maintaining a parallel government.
Later that year, he successfully led a campaign which blocked the introduction of five million zaire banknotes but soldiers went on a looting spree when paid in the notes.
The rebellion in eastern Zaire changed the balance of power in Zaire and Mobutu was forced to reappoint his chief rival last week after parliament nominated Tshisekedi.
Born on December 14, 1932, in the central city of Kananga, Tshisekedi trained as a lawyer and graduated from the Catholic Lovanium University in Kinshasa in 1961.
As interior minister from 1965, when Mobutu seized power, until 1968, he helped write the N'Sele Manifesto which laid the groundwork for Zaire's conversion to single-party rule.
He served as justice minister and planning minister before going to Morocco as ambassador in 1969. He was later deputy speaker of parliament and chairman of state airline, Air Zaire.

Tshisekedi started speaking out against the government in 1980 as a founding member of the Group of 13, an organisation of parliamentarians who published a letter to Mobutu condemning government corruption and calling for democratic reforms.
He was arrested in 1982 and sentenced to 15 years in prison for treason. He was released the following year after protests from Amnesty International and other human rights groups.
From time to time thereafter, Tshisekedi was placed under house arrest or imprisoned for mounting anti-Mobutu protests.
At one point the government announced he had been placed in a mental institution after trying to stage a demonstration against Mobutu in the capital.
He has been married to Marthe Kasalu since 1961. They have six sons.
